title: About Statigami
text:
I’m a sports fan, but I’m also a statistician. And I often find myself thinking about both sides of the story.
I’ll be watching a football game, celebrating a touchdown, and at the same time wondering how much that touchdown actually means. Is my team really playing that well? Or is this just something that happens sometimes?
That’s kind of how my brain works.
I love the excitement of sports. The big plays, the upsets, the games that make you think something unbelievable is happening. But I also like looking at the numbers and asking whether they tell the same story.
That’s where Statigami comes in.
Inspired by Scorigami, Statigami started as a fun idea to explore interesting and unusual patterns in sports. I created a GitHub repository, started asking questions, and began turning some of those questions into data projects.
Some ideas come from watching games on TV. Others come from being at the ballpark and noticing something I want to investigate.
I’m not always trying to prove a point. Most of the time, I’m just curious.

title: About Statigami
text:
Why I share it
I grew up in a family that loves watching and talking about sports. Some of my favorite parts of being a fan are the conversations about what happened, why it happened, and what might happen next.
Statigami is another way for me to have those conversations.
I enjoy reading sports articles that go beyond the final score, especially ones that uncover something interesting in the data. And I figure there are probably other people who enjoy those stories too.
Not every analysis needs to solve a business problem or lead to some practical decision. Sometimes a question is worth exploring simply because it’s interesting.
I want to make things that I would read.
And if other people enjoy them too, even better.

title: About Statigami
text:
A little about me
I’m Jackson, a Statistics: Data Science student at Brigham Young University.
I enjoy statistics, programming, and finding creative ways to use data to answer questions. Statigami is a personal project where I can bring those interests together with my love of sports.
It’s also a place for me to experiment, learn new things, and share what I discover along the way.
I’m still figuring out exactly what Statigami will become. For now, I’m just having fun asking questions and seeing where the data takes me.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
text:
// NFL · 2019-2025 · 84 NTED games · N=493 tight end games
The NFL has a holiday for tight ends. Every year on the fourth Sunday of October, the league celebrates National Tight Ends Day (NTED). So here is the obvious question: do tight ends actually play better that day?
My favorite NFL player is George Kittle, and my favorite team is the San Francisco 49ers. Kittle has been a big part of popularizing National Tight Ends Day, and he’s done a lot for tight ends off the field too: in 2021 he organized the first Tight End University in Nashville with Travis Kelce and Greg Olsen, an offseason get-together for tight ends from around the league. So with NTED coming up, I thought it’d be cool to see whether there’s actually some correlation between the celebration and how tight ends play. Just for fun, see if it’s actually a thing.
Short answer: not that I can find. Teams don’t throw to their tight ends any more than usual on NTED. But the day has produced some huge individual games, and a few tight ends have records on it that look almost too good. Most of that looks like what chance alone would produce.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: What National Tight Ends Day is
text:
What National Tight Ends Day is
According to the San Francisco 49ers, the name was born in Week 2 of 2018, when 49ers tight end Garrett Celek caught an 11-yard touchdown from Jimmy Garoppolo against Detroit, and it was Garoppolo who coined it. The NFL then made the fourth Sunday of October the official date. The Pro Football Hall of Fame marks October 27, 2019 as the first official league-wide National Tight Ends Day.
That gives seven official NTEDs to study: 2019 through 2025.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
text:
How this was measured
The comparison that matters is not “tight ends on NTED vs tight ends in general”. Tight ends’ share of the passing game has been rising: from 20.8% of team targets in 2019 to 23.9% in 2025. So every NTED is compared with other Sundays in the same season.

NTED games are games played on the NTED Sunday itself: 84 games over seven seasons. Thursday and Monday games in the same NFL week are left out (they are checked separately below).
Team usage is a team’s tight end share of its targets: every tight end counted, backups included.
Individual tight ends are compared with their own average on other Sundays that season, for the same team, using only games they actually played. A game a player missed is never counted as a zero.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: Teams don’t throw to tight ends more on NTED
text:
Teams don’t throw to tight ends more on NTED



League-wide share of team targets on every Sunday of each regular season, by position group. The NTED Sunday (gold) sits inside the normal spread of ordinary Sundays (blue) every year.


On a league-wide basis, the tight end share of targets on NTED averaged almost exactly what a typical Sunday produced (−0.04 percentage points vs the median Sunday). NTED was above the median Sunday in three of seven seasons. In 2024 it ranked second of 18 Sundays; in 2025 it ranked last.



Each team’s tight end share of targets on NTED minus its share on its other Sundays that season. Season averages (gold) sit close to zero.


Team by team, the picture is the same. Across 168 team games on NTED, the tight end share of targets was 0.4 points higher than each team’s own baseline, with a 95% interval of −0.8 to +1.5 points. 51% of teams were above their baseline: a coin flip.
Honestly, as a statistician, that’s what I expected. It’s just another Sunday, you know? I didn’t think National Tight Ends Day would change play calls or decide who gets open. I wondered if maybe there was some kind of hot streak happening, but I figured it would probably be random. So I wasn’t surprised, I was just curious.
What it did make me wonder about is Kittle, because he actually does seem to have better games on NTED. More on him below.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: Individual tight ends: same targets, a few more yards
text:
Individual tight ends: same targets, a few more yards



Distribution of each tight end’s NTED targets and receiving yards minus his own average on other Sundays that season. Bars shade from blue (below baseline) to gold (above).


Across 493 tight end games, NTED targets were exactly in line with each player’s normal workload (−0.01 per game). Receiving yards were slightly higher: about 2 yards per player above baseline (95% interval: 0.3 to 3.7).
That yardage bump is the one result in this analysis that looks unusual, so it gets a closer look below.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: Reality check: what if every Sunday were NTED?
text:
Reality check: what if every Sunday were NTED?
The strongest test is a placebo: run the exact same comparison for every ordinary Sunday, as if each one were National Tight Ends Day, and see whether the real NTED stands out.



Average change in team tight end target share for every Sunday of each season. NTED (gold) lands anywhere from near the top to dead last.


For team usage it doesn’t. A random set of seven ordinary Sundays, one per season, matches or beats NTED 40% of the time.
For receiving yards, the real NTED does look unusual at first: only 2% of random Sunday sets match its average. But that average leans on three huge games:

Take out Travis Kelce’s 179 yards in 2023, Kyle Pitts’s 163 in 2021 and Tucker Kraft’s 143 in 2025, and NTED looks like any other Sunday. The typical tight end actually gains a little less than usual on NTED. With about ten measures tested, one standing out is roughly what chance alone would produce.
The result also holds when NTED is compared only with nearby Sundays (within three weeks), when Thursday and Monday games of NTED week are included, when each opponent’s usual tight end defense is accounted for, and when any single season is left out.
Again, I think it’s probably just random. But who knows? Maybe National Tight Ends Day has inspired some tight ends to go out, get open, and work extra hard to make it a special day for them. Kelce, Pitts and Kraft are established tight ends who’ve had big games outside of NTED too, so randomness is the easy explanation. But who’s to say randomness is what made them have those games, and not that they were motivated by National Tight Ends Day?
These numbers can’t tell motivation apart from luck, so that’s me talking as a fan, not a finding. Maybe a few got the memo, some didn’t.

Across his five NTED Sundays, Kittle has averaged 82 receiving yards against 67 in his usual games those seasons, with a touchdown in each of his last three NTED Sundays. Random games from the same seasons would produce a record that strong about 1 time in 10: a genuinely good run, but not one that rules out luck.
Two oddities: he did not play on NTED in 2021, and in 2023 the 49ers played on Monday night, so Kittle’s NTED-week game was not on National Tight Ends Day itself.
I have two takes on this, and they don’t totally agree.
As a 49ers fan: absolutely, I think he’s trying to ball out on National Tight Ends Day. I’m sure it’s something in the back of his mind, like, “I’m gonna go out and get it.” He’s said that “every day is National Tight Ends Day.” I imagine Brock Purdy looking for him even more that day (Purdy was his quarterback for the 128-yard game in 2024), and Purdy, McCaffrey, Juszczyk and the rest of the guys wanting him to have a big game. They love Kittle. They’re all bros, and they want to have a good day on National Tight Ends Day. That’s my impression from the outside, not something I actually know about what his teammates are thinking.
As a statistician: there are plenty of football explanations that have nothing to do with the calendar. Maybe the 49ers played teams that were weaker at defending tight ends. Maybe the opposing linebackers were injured or just struggled against him. Maybe the play calling or the matchup favored Kittle, or injuries and players coming back changed the way defenses covered him. And with only five NTED Sundays, a run this good shows up about 1 time in 10 by chance anyway.
Maybe mindset is part of the story. I just can’t show that with these numbers.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: The NTED standouts, and the luck behind them
text:
The NTED standouts, and the luck behind them



Average NTED receiving yards vs usual games in the same seasons, for the ten tight ends with the strongest NTED records plus George Kittle.


Among the 28 receiving tight ends with at least three NTEDs (and at least three targets in a usual game), a few have remarkable records:

Hayden Hurst: above his usual yards in all three of his NTEDs.
Cade Otton: above his usual in all four.
Logan Thomas: three for three.
Kyle Pitts: four of five, averaging 74 NTED yards against 44 in his usual games.

Here is the catch. Give 28 players a handful of games each, and some will string together great ones by chance. About three of these 28 would be expected to post an NTED record this strong by luck alone. Four did.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: What the day is really about
text:
What the day is really about
My favorite NTED memory isn’t a stat line. I remember seeing a video of Kittle mic’d up on National Tight Ends Day, and what stuck with me most was how excited he was about the celebration, and how much he’s done for the position’s identity. (NFL.com has a Mic’d Up from the 49ers’ NTED win over the Panthers in 2019.)
That got me thinking about something bigger. Maybe tight ends haven’t played substantially better, or even significantly better, on National Tight Ends Day, but tight ends have changed the game of football. I think about guys like George Kittle, Travis Kelce, Tony Gonzalez and Vernon Davis. The modern tight end feels like a wide receiver and an offensive lineman in one: they can block, run routes, catch passes, and completely change what an offense can do. Now every tight end is basically a wide receiver lineman, right?
Kittle embodies that for me. He loves blocking, he loves catching the football, and he loves being a good teammate. They’re all just like the best teammates, from what it seems like on the outside.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
section: So, do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
text:
So, do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
Not in any way the data can detect. Across seven seasons, teams gave their tight ends the same share of the passing game on NTED as on any other Sunday, and individual tight ends saw the same number of targets. A small bump in receiving yards traces back to a few outstanding games rather than a league-wide pattern. That’s not proof the day has zero effect, but if there is one, it’s too small to stand out from an ordinary Sunday.
To me, that doesn’t make the day meaningless. It might not change the stats, but it’s a celebration of the position, how much it has developed, and players like Kittle who have helped build its identity. I want people to appreciate how important tight ends have become to NFL offenses.
One thing I started wondering about while looking at the position data: have tight ends been taking over some of the short passing game that used to go to running backs? Even in these seven seasons, tight ends went from 20.8% of team targets to 23.9%, while running backs went from 20.6% to 17.9%. Seven seasons isn’t a 10- or 20-year trend, though, so that one’s a question for a future Statigami project.
So this Sunday, watch the tight ends. Like, see what they do. Focus on them a little bit more than usual this time: your favorite tight end, or your team’s tight end. See how they help your team.

title: Do tight ends play better on National Tight Ends Day?
text:
Data and methods






NoteData, definitions and limitations





Data. Weekly player stats, schedules, snap counts and rosters from nflverse via the nflreadr R package, used under CC BY 4.0. Snap counts originally from Pro Football Reference. Regular season only, 2019-2025.
NTED games. Games played on the fourth Sunday of October, matched on the actual game date. Thursday and Monday games in the same NFL week are excluded from the main analysis and tested separately.
Who counts as a tight end. The team’s roster position for that season (some players change positions over their careers). Taysom Hill is counted as a tight end.
Games played vs missed. Weekly stats only include players who recorded a stat, so snap counts are used to identify everyone who played. A tight end who played but was not targeted counts as zero targets; a tight end who did not play is left out rather than counted as zero.
Uncertainty. 95% intervals come from a bootstrap that resamples whole games. The “random Sunday” comparisons draw one ordinary Sunday per season, 10,000 times.
Limitations. Seven seasons is a small sample, and this is observational: it can show whether NTED looks different, not why. Touchdowns are too rare to analyze on their own.
Code: national-tight-ends-day/analysis.R.
